etymology: The descendants of Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn by Leah, whose name means see, a son. Firstborn by birth and disinherited by conduct, Reuben’s children settled the high pastureland east of Jordan and were the first tribe of Israel carried into captivity.
biblical_def: The Reubenites are the children of Israel’s firstborn, and their whole history is governed by a sentence spoken over their father on Jacob’s deathbed: Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed (Genesis 49:4). The birthright passed to Joseph’s sons, the priesthood to Levi, the sceptre to Judah. When Israel reached the plains of Moab, the Reubenites and the Gadites saw that the land of Jazer and Gilead was good for cattle and asked to be settled there: bring us not over Jordan (Numbers 32:5). Moses met the request with the question every generation should be asked — Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here? — and with the warning be sure your sin will find you out. They agreed to cross armed before their brethren and did so, and the land east of Jordan was theirs (Deuteronomy 3:12). But the choice had a long shadow. They built the great altar Ed by Jordan because they feared their children would one day be told What have ye to do with the LORD God of Israel? (Joshua 22:24). Their fear was not idle: the eastern tribes were the first to be swept away, when the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria… and he carried them away, even the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 5:26).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no REUBENITE entry. The name Reuben is Hebrew, see, a son, from Leah’s cry at his birth (Genesis 29:32), and the gentilic follows the ordinary Hebrew formation.
webster_full: REUBENITE, n. — A descendant of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob; one of the tribe settled east of Jordan.
Genesis 29:32 explains the name: She called his name Reuben: for she said, Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction.
The tribe’s inheritance lay from the Arnon northward through the plain country (Deuteronomy 3:12, 16).
Bezer in the wilderness was their city of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8).
Webster 1828 does not carry biblical gentilics of this kind; the sense is fixed by Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Chronicles.
scriptures: Genesis 49:4
Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed; then defiledst thou it: he went up to my couch.
Numbers 32:6
And Moses said unto the children of Gad and to the children of Reuben, Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here?
Numbers 32:23
But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.
Deuteronomy 3:12
And this land, which we possessed at that time, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, and half mount Gilead, and the cities thereof, gave I unto the Reubenites and to the Gadites.
1 Chronicles 5:26

And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day.
corruption_summary: Numbers 32:23 is quoted constantly and almost always as a threat of exposure — the sin that will be found out. Moses is saying something graver: the sin itself will hunt the sinner down.
corruption_paragraphs: Be sure your sin will find you out is not a warning that someone will discover what you did. The Hebrew has the sin as the subject and the sinner as the object; it comes after him. That is why the phrase stands where it does, in a negotiation about settling short of the promised inheritance. Reuben and Gad did keep their word and cross armed; the sin Moses feared was not merely broken promise but the choice of good pasture over the land God had given, and that choice found them out four centuries later on the road to Halah and Habor. Sin is not chiefly dangerous because it may be reported. It is dangerous because it pursues, and because the pursuit is often generational and slow.

The second matter is the tribe’s founding disqualification. Reuben was the firstborn and lost the birthright by an act of sexual sin against his father’s household, and Jacob names it on his deathbed without euphemism. He is also the brother who tried to save Joseph from the pit and who offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin — a man of real impulses and no stability. Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel. Scripture’s estimate of such a character is not that he lacked sincerity but that he lacked constancy, and constancy is what a firstborn must have. The New Testament word for it is steadfastness, and James applies the same figure to the doubting man, who is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
roots_summary: Hebrew Reuben (H7205), see, a son, from ra’ah to see and ben a son; the gentilic is Reubeni (H7206).
roots_lines: Hebrew Reuben (H7205) — Reuben; Leah’s firstborn, named at Genesis 29:32.
Hebrew Reubeni (H7206) — Reubenite; the gentilic used from Numbers 26:7 through 1 Chronicles.
Hebrew pachaz (H6349) — unbridled, wanton, unstable; the word behind unstable as water (Genesis 49:4).
Hebrew Ed — witness; the name given the altar by Jordan (Joshua 22:34), for it shall be a witness between us.
Hebrew Betser (H1221) — Bezer; the Reubenite city of refuge in the wilderness plain (Deuteronomy 4:43).
usage: Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here? (Numbers 32:6) — Moses’ question to a tribe that wanted to settle early.
Be sure your sin will find you out (Numbers 32:23) — the sin, not the rumour, does the finding.
He carried them away, even the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 5:26) — the first of Israel to go into exile.

etymology: The descendants of Gad, Jacob’s son by Zilpah, whose name Leah explained as a troop cometh. A frontier tribe on the exposed eastern border, they became Israel’s hardened soldiers, and the Chronicler’s description of the Gadites who came to David at Ziklag is one of the finest military portraits in Scripture.
biblical_def: The Gadites held the tableland east of Jordan from the Arnon to the Jabbok, with Ramoth in Gilead as their city of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43). They asked Moses with Reuben for that land because of their cattle, took the rebuke, and pledged to go over armed before their brethren; Moses gave them the territory on that condition (Deuteronomy 3:16). Their position on the frontier made them fighters. The Chronicler records that when David was hiding in the hold, there separated themselves unto David… of the Gadites men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and were as swift as the roes upon the mountains, and that they crossed Jordan in the first month when it had overflown all his banks. That is the tribe’s character: exposed ground, constant war, and a readiness to swim a flooded river to reach a rejected king. Jacob’s blessing had already given the shape of it — a troop shall overcome him, but he shall overcome at the last. The eastern position that made them soldiers also made them the first to fall, and 1 Chronicles 5:26 carries the Gadites away with Reuben and half Manasseh under Assyria.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no GADITE entry. The Hebrew Gad means a troop or fortune, and Genesis 30:11 turns on the word: A troop cometh: and she called his name Gad.
webster_full: GADITE, n. — A descendant of Gad, the son of Jacob by Zilpah; one of the tribe settled east of Jordan in Gilead.
Genesis 30:11 gives the naming: And Leah said, A troop cometh: and she called his name Gad.
Jacob’s blessing plays on the same root: Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last (Genesis 49:19).
Ramoth in Gilead, their city of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43), became the contested frontier fortress where Ahab died.
A prophet named Gad, David’s seer, is a different person entirely (1 Samuel 22:5; 2 Samuel 24:11).
scriptures: Numbers 32:1
Now the children of Reuben and the children of Gad had a very great multitude of cattle: and when they saw the land of Jazer, and the land of Gilead, that, behold, the place was a place for cattle;
Numbers 32:5
Wherefore, said they, if we have found grace in thy sight, let this land be given unto thy servants for a possession, and bring us not over Jordan.
Deuteronomy 3:16
And unto the Reubenites and unto the Gadites I gave from Gilead even unto the river Arnon half the valley, and the border even unto the river Jabbok, which is the border of the children of Ammon;
Joshua 13:8
With whom the Reubenites and the Gadites have received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond Jordan eastward, even as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them;
2 Kings 10:33
From Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a good request granted on the wrong side of the river is still a real loss, and that courage on the frontier does not make up for choosing the frontier.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson wanting recovery is the difference between a lawful request and a wise one. The land east of Jordan was genuinely good for cattle, the Gadites genuinely kept their pledge to fight for their brethren, and Moses genuinely granted the petition. Nothing in the transaction was forbidden. Yet the tribe spent its history as a border garrison, exposed to Ammon, Moab, and Syria in turn, and it went into captivity first. Scripture records this without a single word of condemnation, which is exactly what makes it instructive. Believers are constantly presented with permissible choices that place them outside the centre of what God has given, and a permitted arrangement can cost a family three generations.

The second thing to see is the honour the Chronicler pays them anyway. Men of might, faces like lions, swift as roes on the mountains, crossing Jordan in flood to reach David in the hold — that is written of the very tribe that had once asked not to cross Jordan at all. God is not stingy with commendation toward people whose earlier choices He had to correct. The same book that records the exile of the Gadites records their valour, and both are true. A Christian who has settled for less than he should have is not thereby disqualified from courage; he is called to it where he stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gad (H1410), a troop or fortune, from gadad to crowd or invade; the gentilic is Gadi (H1425).
roots_lines: Hebrew Gad (H1410) — Gad; a troop, from Leah’s a troop cometh (Genesis 30:11).
Hebrew gadad (H1413) — to crowd, to gather in troops, to invade; the root of the wordplay in Genesis 49:19.
Hebrew Gadi (H1425) — Gadite; the gentilic of Deuteronomy 3 and Joshua 13.
Hebrew Ramoth Gilead — Ramoth in Gilead, the Gadite city of refuge and the fortress where Ahab fell (1 Kings 22).
Hebrew Yabboq (H2999) — the Jabbok; their northern border and the brook where Jacob wrestled.
usage: Bring us not over Jordan (Numbers 32:5) — the request that shaped a tribe’s whole history.
Unto the Reubenites and unto the Gadites I gave from Gilead (Deuteronomy 3:16) — the grant made on the frontier.
The Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites (2 Kings 10:33) — the first territory Hazael took from Israel.

etymology: The descendants of Simeon, Jacob’s second son by Leah, whose name means hearing. Cursed with Levi for the massacre at Shechem and sentenced to be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel, they received no separate territory but an inheritance swallowed inside Judah.
biblical_def: The Simeonites are the tribe whose history is the visible working out of a curse. Jacob said of Simeon and Levi, instruments of cruelty are in their habitations… Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:5, 7). It happened exactly so, and it happened twice over in opposite directions. Levi was scattered too, but scattered as the priestly tribe among forty-eight cities, the curse turned into a ministry after Phinehas stood up at Peor. Simeon was scattered without that reversal: their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah (Joshua 19:1), a tribe absorbed into a greater one. The tribe’s worst moment is recorded in the same chapter that redeemed Levi’s: the man slain with the Midianitish woman at Peor was Zimri, the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites (Numbers 25:14). Their numbers collapsed from fifty-nine thousand at the first census to twenty-two thousand at the second. Moses’ blessing in Deuteronomy 33 does not name Simeon at all. Yet the tribe is not erased: Simeon stands sealed in Revelation 7, twelve thousand of them, in the roll of the redeemed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no SIMEONITE entry. The Hebrew Shimon means hearing, from Leah’s word at his birth, Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated (Genesis 29:33).
webster_full: SIMEONITE, n. — A descendant of Simeon, the second son of Jacob by Leah.
Genesis 29:33 gives the naming: the LORD had heard that Leah was hated, and she called his name Simeon.
Their inheritance lay inside Judah’s portion in the far south — Beersheba, Ziklag, and the cities of the Negeb (Joshua 19:1-9).
The Simeon of Luke 2 who took the child Jesus in his arms, and Simeon called Niger of Acts 13:1, are unrelated individuals bearing the same common name.
Webster 1828 does not carry the gentilic; the sense comes from Genesis 49, Numbers 25-26, and Joshua 19.
scriptures: Genesis 49:5
Simeon and Levi are brethren; instruments of cruelty are in their habitations.
Genesis 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
Numbers 25:14
Now the name of the Israelite that was slain, even that was slain with the Midianitish woman, was Zimri, the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites.
Numbers 26:14
These are the families of the Simeonites, twenty and two thousand and two hundred.
Joshua 19:1
And the second lot came forth to Simeon, even for the tribe of the children of Simeon according to their families: and their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah.
corruption_summary: Jacob’s curse on Simeon and Levi is often softened into a comment on temperament. It is a sentence, it was executed, and the difference between the two tribes afterward is one of Scripture’s clearest lessons in what repentance does to a judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Simeon and Levi received the identical sentence: divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel. Both were scattered. Only one scattering became a blessing. At Sinai, when Moses asked who was on the LORD’s side, the sons of Levi gathered to him; at Peor, Phinehas the Levite stood up and executed judgment while Zimri the Simeonite prince was the man committing the sin. From that point Levi’s dispersion is priestly service in forty-eight cities and Simeon’s is absorption into Judah. God did not revoke the sentence in either case; He determined what the sentence would mean. This is the doctrine of chastening in Hebrews 12 written across four centuries of tribal history, and it should be preached wherever a Christian assumes that a consequence, once pronounced, has fixed the whole future.

The second thing is the fair-mindedness of the record. Simeon is never rehabilitated in the histories, is passed over in Moses’ blessing, and dwindles from fifty-nine thousand to twenty-two thousand men. And Simeon stands in Revelation 7 among the sealed, twelve thousand strong, with the rest. The final roll of the redeemed is not adjusted for tribal performance. Whatever else the Reformed doctrine of election means, it means that the standing of a people before God at the last is settled by God’s choice and Christ’s work and not by the record they compiled in the meantime.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shimon (H8095), hearing, from shama to hear; the gentilic is Shimoni (H8099).
roots_lines: Hebrew Shimon (H8095) — Simeon; hearing, from Leah’s naming (Genesis 29:33).
Hebrew Shimoni (H8099) — Simeonite; Numbers 25:14, 26:14, 1 Chronicles 27:16.
Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, disperse; the verb of the sentence in Genesis 49:7.
Hebrew Zimri (H2174) — Zimri; the Simeonite prince slain by Phinehas at Peor.
Greek Symeon (G4826) — Simeon; the tribe sealed in Revelation 7:7.
usage: Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce (Genesis 49:7) — Jacob’s sentence on Simeon and Levi.
A prince of a chief house among the Simeonites (Numbers 25:14) — the tribe’s representative at Peor.
Their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah (Joshua 19:1) — the sentence carried out on the map.

etymology: The descendants of Benjamin, Jacob’s youngest, whom Rachel dying called Benoni, son of my sorrow, and whom his father renamed Benjamin, son of the right hand. The smallest tribe, nearly annihilated in Judges, it gave Israel her first king and the church her greatest apostle.
biblical_def: The Benjamites held the narrow hill country between Ephraim and Judah, with Jerusalem on their border and Gibeah, Bethel, Jericho, and Mizpeh within it. Their history swings between extremes. In Judges 19 the men of Gibeah, who were Benjamites, committed the outrage on the Levite’s concubine, and when the tribe refused to give up the offenders, all Israel went to war against them: the LORD smote Benjamin before Israel (Judges 20:35), and six hundred men survived at the rock Rimmon, so that Israel wept, There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day (Judges 21:6). From that remnant came Saul, who said of himself, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? (1 Samuel 9:21), and after him the seven hundred lefthanded slingers who could sling at an hair breadth, and Ehud the deliverer, and Mordecai, and Jeremiah of Anathoth. Benjamin stayed with Judah when the kingdom divided, and so shares the covenant line to Christ’s day. Then, at the end of the canon, the tribe that had nearly been cut off produces Saul of Tarsus, who twice names his lineage as the ground of a boast he counts loss: of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews (Philippians 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no BENJAMITE entry. The Hebrew Binyamin means son of the right hand; Rachel’s name for him, Benoni, means son of my sorrow (Genesis 35:18).
webster_full: BENJAMITE, n. — A descendant of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob; one of the tribe whose lot lay between Ephraim and Judah.
Genesis 35:18 records both names: as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.
Jacob’s blessing is martial: Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey (Genesis 49:27).
The tribe was famous for lefthanded slingers and archers (Judges 20:16; 1 Chronicles 12:2), and for Ehud, a man lefthanded (Judges 3:15).
Webster 1828 does not carry the gentilic; Judges, 1 Samuel, Esther, Romans, and Philippians supply the whole biblical usage.
scriptures: Judges 19:16
And, behold, there came an old man from his work out of the field at even, which was also of mount Ephraim; and he sojourned in Gibeah: but the men of the place were Benjamites.
Judges 20:35
And the LORD smote Benjamin before Israel: and the children of Israel destroyed of the Benjamites that day twenty and five thousand and an hundred men: all these drew the sword.
Judges 21:6
And the children of Israel repented them for Benjamin their brother, and said, There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day.
1 Samuel 9:21
And Saul answered and said, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?
Philippians 3:5
Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;
corruption_summary: Judges 19 through 21 is the passage most often cited to prove the Old Testament barbaric, and it is in fact the book’s own indictment of what happens when every man does that which is right in his own eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: The narrative of Gibeah is told without a single word of approval for anyone in it. The Levite is a coward who puts his concubine out the door; the men of Gibeah are Sodom transplanted into Israel; the tribe defends its criminals out of clan loyalty; the assembled tribes overreact into near-extermination and then contrive a second atrocity to supply wives for the survivors. The book states its own thesis four times, and the last verse of it is the interpretation: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Judges is not modelling behaviour; it is diagnosing a nation without a king, and it is written to make the reader long for one. Reading it as though Scripture endorsed what it records is a failure of ordinary literary attention before it is a failure of theology.

The second thing to see is the trajectory from Gibeah to Tarsus. The tribe that produced the outrage produced the king who spared Agag and hunted David, and then the Pharisee who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning — and that Pharisee became the apostle who wrote Romans. Paul lists his Benjamite descent among the things he counted but dung, that I may win Christ. The tribe of the wolf, nearly cut off, is the one God used to carry the gospel to the Gentiles. That is what grace does with a lineage, and it is the reason no Christian should ever describe any family, tribe, or people as beyond hope.
roots_summary: Hebrew Binyamin (H1144), son of the right hand; Ben Oni, son of my sorrow, was Rachel’s name for him; the gentilic is Ben-yemini (H1145).
roots_lines: Hebrew Binyamin (H1144) — Benjamin; son of the right hand, the hand of strength and favour.
Hebrew Ben Oni (H1126) — Benoni; son of my sorrow, Rachel’s dying name for him (Genesis 35:18).
Hebrew Ben-yemini (H1145) — Benjamite; literally a son of the right hand.
Hebrew itter yad yemino — shut of his right hand; the idiom for lefthanded, used of Ehud (Judges 3:15) and the slingers of Judges 20:16.
Greek Beniamin (G958) — Benjamin; Paul’s tribe (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5) and sealed in Revelation 7:8.
usage: The men of the place were Benjamites (Judges 19:16) — the quiet sentence before the worst chapter in Judges.
There is one tribe cut off from Israel this day (Judges 21:6) — Israel weeping over her own judgment.
Of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews (Philippians 3:5) — the pedigree Paul counted loss for Christ.

etymology: The descendants of Dan, Jacob’s son by Bilhah, whose name means judge. Assigned a lot on the Philistine border they never held, they migrated north, took Laish by the sword, renamed it Dan, and set up a graven image there — the first standing idolatry in Israel and the northern anchor of Jeroboam’s calves.
biblical_def: The Danites are Israel’s cautionary tribe. Their allotted inheritance lay on the coastal plain toward Joppa, hard against the Philistines, and they could not hold it. From Zorah and Eshtaol, of the family of the Danites, came Manoah and his barren wife and the son given them, Samson (Judges 13:2) — a judge who fought the Philistines alone because his tribe would not. Judges 18 then records what the tribe did instead: six hundred men appointed with weapons of war went north, robbed Micah of his ephod and teraphim and his hired Levite, took the quiet unsuspecting city of Laish, burned it, rebuilt it as Dan, and installed the stolen images — and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land (Judges 18:30). That sanctuary stood for centuries; Jeroboam later set one of his golden calves there. Jacob’s blessing had said, Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path (Genesis 49:17). Dan is not named among the sealed tribes of Revelation 7, though Ezekiel 48 gives Dan a portion in the restored land — and the omission has occasioned much sober comment and a good deal of unwarranted speculation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no DANITE entry. The Hebrew Dan means judge, from Rachel’s word at his birth, God hath judged me (Genesis 30:6); the city of Dan gave the proverb from Dan even to Beersheba.
webster_full: DANITE, n. — A descendant of Dan, the son of Jacob by Bilhah; one of the tribe whose lot lay toward the Philistine coast and who afterward settled at Laish in the far north.
Genesis 30:6 gives the naming: And Rachel said, God hath judged me, and hath also heard my voice, and hath given me a son: therefore called she his name Dan.
The northern city of Dan, formerly Laish or Leshem, fixed the proverbial northern limit of the land, from Dan even to Beersheba.
Samson, the tribe’s one judge, was of Zorah, of the family of the Danites (Judges 13:2).
Webster 1828 does not carry the gentilic; Joshua 19, Judges 13-18, and 1 Kings 12 supply the biblical usage.
scriptures: Genesis 49:17
Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path, that biteth the horse heels, so that his rider shall fall backward.
Judges 13:2
And there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not.
Judges 18:11
And there went from thence of the family of the Danites, out of Zorah and out of Eshtaol, six hundred men appointed with weapons of war.
Judges 18:30
And the children of Dan set up the graven image: and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land.
1 Chronicles 12:35
And of the Danites expert in war twenty and eight thousand and six hundred.
corruption_summary: Dan’s absence from the sealed tribes of Revelation 7 has been made to carry an enormous weight of speculation — most notoriously the tradition that Antichrist will arise from Dan — and the text supports none of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Irenaeus reported a tradition, drawn from Jeremiah 8:16 and Genesis 49:17, that the man of sin would come out of Dan, and dispensational writers have kept it alive. Scripture nowhere says so. Revelation 7 omits Dan and lists Manasseh alongside Joseph to keep the number at twelve; the list also omits Ephraim by name. Building a doctrine of Antichrist’s ancestry on an omission is precisely the method the Reformers rejected when they insisted that Scripture interprets Scripture and that what is not plainly set down is not to be pressed on the conscience. Ezekiel 48:1 gives Dan the first portion in the restored land, which no theory of Danite reprobation can absorb.

What the text does say is worth more than the speculation. A tribe that would not fight for the inheritance God gave took an easier one by attacking a quiet people that dwelt careless, and it carried a stolen ephod and a hired priest along with it. Judges 18:30 dates the priesthood of that shrine to the captivity of the land, meaning Dan’s idolatry outlived every man who set it up. Sin planted at a tribe’s founding does not stay a founder’s sin. Jeroboam found a calf-shrine already waiting at Dan four centuries later, and the northern kingdom went into exile with it standing.
roots_summary: Hebrew Dan (H1835), judge, from din (H1777) to judge or plead a cause; the gentilic is Dani (H1839).
roots_lines: Hebrew Dan (H1835) — Dan; a judge, from Rachel’s God hath judged me (Genesis 30:6).
Hebrew din (H1777) — to judge, to contend, to plead a cause; the root of the name.
Hebrew Dani (H1839) — Danite; Judges 13:2, 18:11, 1 Chronicles 12:35.
Hebrew Layish (H3919) — Laish, a lion; the quiet city taken and renamed Dan (Judges 18:29).
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; the children of Dan set up the graven image (Judges 18:30).
usage: Dan shall be a serpent by the way (Genesis 49:17) — Jacob’s word over the tribe.
Six hundred men appointed with weapons of war (Judges 18:11) — the migration that took an easier inheritance.
The children of Dan set up the graven image (Judges 18:30) — a shrine that outlasted the men who built it.

etymology: The descendants of Ephraim, Joseph’s younger son, whom Jacob deliberately blessed above Manasseh with crossed hands. Their name means doubly fruitful, and their tribe became so dominant in the north that the prophets use Ephraim as the standing name for the whole northern kingdom.
biblical_def: The Ephraimites are the leading tribe of the north, and Scripture’s portrait of them is of great gifts joined to a chronic quarrelsomeness. Jacob crossed his hands over Joseph’s sons and gave the greater blessing to the younger: truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations (Genesis 48:19). Joshua was an Ephraimite, and the tabernacle stood in their territory at Shiloh for centuries. But they failed the first test of the conquest — they drave not out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer: but the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites unto this day (Joshua 16:10) — and they spent the era of the judges complaining of being left out of other men’s battles. They chid with Gideon sharply for not calling them (Judges 8:1); they threatened to burn Jephthah’s house over his head, and at the passages of Jordan their own dialect betrayed them: Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth… and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand (Judges 12:6). Jeroboam was an Ephrathite of Zereda, and after him Ephraim is Hosea’s and Isaiah’s name for the apostate northern kingdom — Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned (Hosea 7:8). Isaiah promises the healing of the ancient quarrel: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no EPHRAIMITE entry. The Hebrew Ephrayim is a dual form meaning double fruitfulness, explained at Genesis 41:52: God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.
webster_full: EPHRAIMITE, n. — A descendant of Ephraim, the younger son of Joseph; a member of the chief tribe of the northern kingdom.
Genesis 41:52 supplies the naming: Joseph called the second son Ephraim, For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.
Mount Ephraim, the central highland, held Shiloh, Shechem, Bethel, and Timnathserah where Joshua was buried.
In Hosea, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, Ephraim commonly denotes the whole northern kingdom of the ten tribes.
The word Shibboleth, an ear of corn or a flowing stream, entered English from Judges 12:6 as the name for any test-word that betrays an outsider.
scriptures: Genesis 48:19

And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.
Joshua 16:10
And they drave not out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer: but the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites unto this day, and serve under tribute.
Judges 8:1
And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.
Judges 12:6

Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand.
Hosea 7:8
Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned.
corruption_summary: Hosea’s image of a cake not turned — burnt on one side, raw on the other — is the sharpest description in Scripture of the half-converted religion that is now the default in the English-speaking church.
corruption_paragraphs: A cake not turned is scorched where it faced the fire and uncooked where it did not. Hosea means an Ephraim zealous in one department of religion and untouched in another: keeping the feasts and keeping the calves, courting Egypt and courting Assyria, energetic and useless. The condition is not hypocrisy, which knows itself; the next verse says gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not. The modern equivalents are easy to name and unpleasant to hear — passionate about doctrine and cold at home, generous in public and dishonest in business, orthodox on paper and prayerless. The remedy Hosea preaches is not more heat on the same side. It is repentance, which is being turned.

The Ephraimite temper is the second thing worth naming, because churches reproduce it constantly. Twice the tribe arrives after a battle it did not fight to complain of not being invited, and the second time it costs forty-two thousand lives at the fords. Gideon answered them softly and turned away wrath; Jephthah answered them in kind and the river ran with their dead. Proverbs was not yet written, but the two chapters together are a commentary on it. A man’s wounded standing is one of the most destructive forces in the life of a congregation, and the reason it does so much damage is that it always presents itself as a concern for the work.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ephrayim (H669), double fruitfulness, from parah to be fruitful; the gentilic Ephrathi (H673) serves both for Ephraimite and for Ephrathite of Bethlehem.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ephrayim (H669) — Ephraim; a dual form, double fruitfulness (Genesis 41:52).
Hebrew parah (H6509) — to bear fruit, to be fruitful; the root of the name.
Hebrew Ephrathi (H673) — Ephraimite, and also Ephrathite; context distinguishes the tribe from the men of Bethlehem Ephratah.
Hebrew shibboleth (H7641) — an ear of corn, or a flowing stream; the test-word of Judges 12:6.
Hebrew ugah beli hafukah — a cake not turned (Hosea 7:8), a flat loaf burnt on one side and raw on the other.
usage: The Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites unto this day (Joshua 16:10) — the conquest left unfinished in the strongest tribe.
Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth (Judges 12:6) — the syllable that cost forty-two thousand men.
Ephraim is a cake not turned (Hosea 7:8) — half-baked religion named by a prophet.

etymology: The descendants of Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, whose name means forgetting — God hath made me forget all my toil (Genesis 41:51). Alone among the tribes, Manasseh was divided by the Jordan, half settled in Bashan and Gilead and half in the hill country west of the river.
biblical_def: The Manassites are the one tribe with an inheritance on both sides of Jordan. Half of them took Bashan and northern Gilead with Reuben and Gad; Golan in Bashan was their city of refuge of the Manassites (Deuteronomy 4:43). The other half received the highland north of Ephraim. Jacob had crossed his hands and set the younger brother first, and Joseph objected; Israel answered, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he (Genesis 48:19). Manasseh is therefore the tribe that lives permanently under a blessing that is real and second. From western Manasseh came Gideon of Abiezer; from the east came Jair and the mighty men of Gilead. But the division cost them. When Hazael began cutting Israel short, the first ground he took was theirs: from Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites (2 Kings 10:33). When Assyria came, they were carried away with Reuben and Gad. And the daughters of Zelophehad, who came before Moses to plead their father’s inheritance and won it, were Manassites — the case that fixed Israel’s law of daughters’ succession.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no MANASSITE entry. The Hebrew Menashsheh means causing to forget, from Joseph’s words at the birth of his firstborn in Egypt.
webster_full: MANASSITE, n. — A descendant of Manasseh, the elder son of Joseph; one of the tribe divided between Bashan and the hill country west of Jordan.
Genesis 41:51 gives the naming: And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father’s house.
Golan in Bashan was the Manassite city of refuge east of Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8).
The daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — were of Manasseh (Numbers 27:1; 36:11).
Manasseh king of Judah, the son of Hezekiah, is an entirely different person of the same name.
scriptures: Genesis 48:19

And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.
Deuteronomy 4:43
Namely, Bezer in the wilderness, in the plain country, of the Reubenites; and Ramoth in Gilead, of the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan, of the Manassites.
Deuteronomy 29:8
And we took their land, and gave it for an inheritance unto the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to the half tribe of Manasseh.
Joshua 17:17
And Joshua spake unto the house of Joseph, even to Ephraim and to Manasseh, saying, Thou art a great people, and hast great power: thou shalt not have one lot only:
2 Kings 10:33
From Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is contentment under a real blessing that is nevertheless not the first — the exact discipline the elder brother in Luke 15 refused.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Manasseh was the firstborn and was blessed second, and his father Joseph tried to correct Jacob’s hands and was told, I know it, my son, I know it. The blessing on Manasseh was not withheld or diminished: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. It simply was not the greater. Scripture is full of this arrangement — Leah and Rachel, Aaron and Moses, Martha and Mary, the disciple whom Jesus loved and the rest — and it is one of the hardest providences to receive without bitterness. The elder brother of Luke 15 had never lost anything and could not bear the celebration of one who had, which is the corrupt form of exactly this test.

The second lesson is the cost of a divided position. Manasseh alone straddled the Jordan, and the eastern half took the first blow from Syria, the first blow from Assyria, and the first captivity. Joshua 22 shows the western tribes ready to make war on their eastern brethren over an altar they had misread — a quarrel produced entirely by the distance. Divided settlements produce divided loyalties, and a family or a church spread thin across two commitments will find, when pressure comes, that the far half is taken first. The daughters of Zelophehad, by contrast, came and asked for a definite inheritance in a definite place, and God said, The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.
roots_summary: Hebrew Menashsheh (H4519), causing to forget, from nashah (H5382) to forget; the gentilic is Menashshi (H4520).
roots_lines: Hebrew Menashsheh (H4519) — Manasseh; causing to forget (Genesis 41:51).
Hebrew nashah (H5382) — to forget, to deprive of memory; the root of the name.
Hebrew Menashshi (H4520) — Manassite; Deuteronomy 4:43 and 2 Kings 10:33.
Hebrew Golan (H1474) — Golan; the Manassite city of refuge in Bashan.
Hebrew Tselophchad (H6765) — Zelophehad; the Manassite whose five daughters secured the law of female inheritance (Numbers 27, 36).
usage: Golan in Bashan, of the Manassites (Deuteronomy 4:43) — a city of refuge east of Jordan.
Thou art a great people, and hast great power (Joshua 17:17) — Joshua’s answer to the house of Joseph.
The Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites (2 Kings 10:33) — the eastern tribes taken first.

etymology: The descendants of Kohath, Levi’s second son, comprising the families of the Amramites, Izeharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites (Numbers 3:27). Aaron’s house was Kohathite; so were Moses, Korah, Samuel, and Heman the singer.
biblical_def: The Kohathites are the Levitical clan charged with the holiest burden of the tabernacle. When the camp set forward, Aaron and his sons covered the ark, the table, the candlestick, and the altars, and after that, the sons of Kohath shall come to bear it: but they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die (Numbers 4:15). Their service was carried, not carted: unto the sons of Kohath he gave none of the wagons, because the service of the sanctuary belonging unto them was that they should bear upon their shoulders (Numbers 7:9). That single verse is the standing rebuke of David’s new cart, which cost Uzzah his life, and David afterward said so: None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites: for them hath the LORD chosen to carry the ark of God (1 Chronicles 15:2). Their honour was also their danger. Moses is warned, Cut ye not off the tribe of the families of the Kohathites from among the Levites (Numbers 4:18) — the nearer the service, the sharper the peril, and Korah, a Kohathite, proved it by demanding the priesthood itself. In David’s reordering, Heman the singer of the sons of the Kohathites was set over the service of song, and Kohathite psalms — the sons of Korah — stand in the Psalter to this day.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no KOHATHITE entry. The Hebrew Qehath is of uncertain meaning, sometimes explained as assembly; the family name is used throughout Numbers, Joshua, and Chronicles.
webster_full: KOHATHITE, n. — A descendant of Kohath, the second son of Levi; one of the Levitical clan charged with bearing the sanctuary furniture.
Numbers 3:27 names their four families: the Amramites, the Izeharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites.
Amram was Kohath’s son and the father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (Exodus 6:18, 20), so the priesthood itself is Kohathite.
They pitched on the south side of the tabernacle, under Elizaphan the son of Uzziel (Numbers 3:29-30).
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; Numbers 3-4, Joshua 21, and 1 Chronicles 6 supply the whole usage.
scriptures: Numbers 3:27
And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites.
Numbers 4:15

And when Aaron and his sons have made an end of covering the sanctuary, and all the vessels of the sanctuary, as the camp is to set forward; after that, the sons of Kohath shall come to bear it: but they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die. These things are the burden of the sons of Kohath in the tabernacle of the congregation.
Numbers 4:18
Cut ye not off the tribe of the families of the Kohathites from among the Levites:
Numbers 7:9
But unto the sons of Kohath he gave none: because the service of the sanctuary belonging unto them was that they should bear upon their shoulders.
1 Chronicles 15:2
Then David said, None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites: for them hath the LORD chosen to carry the ark of God, and to minister unto him for ever.
corruption_summary: Numbers 7:9 is the Old Testament’s clearest statement of the regulative principle in practice: God appointed how the holy things were to be moved, and the appointment was shoulders, not wheels.
corruption_paragraphs: David’s first attempt to bring up the ark was sincere, joyful, well attended, and accompanied by music, and it killed a man. The new cart was a Philistine method; the Philistines had used one, and it had worked for them, because God was not judging them by a law they had never received. Israel had the law, and the law said shoulders. When David tried again he said so plainly: the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order. The due order is the point. What God has commanded in His worship is required; what He has not commanded is not admitted, however successful it looks elsewhere and however earnest the people carrying it. The Kohathites are the regulative principle with poles on their shoulders.

The second thing is the double edge of nearness. The Kohathites bore the ark and were told they would die if they touched or even looked upon the holy things uncovered, and Moses is warned not to let them be cut off. Korah was a Kohathite who already had the highest carrying office in Israel and wanted the censer as well. Privilege in the things of God does not satisfy an ungoverned heart; it feeds it. That is why the New Testament warns that teachers receive the greater condemnation, and why the men nearest the pulpit need the plainest accountability. The ones in real danger at the tabernacle were never the men at the back of the camp.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qehath (H6955), Kohath; the gentilic Qehathi (H6956); their charge was the qodesh, the holy things, borne on the shoulder.
roots_lines: Hebrew Qehath (H6955) — Kohath; second son of Levi (Genesis 46:11; Exodus 6:16).
Hebrew Qehathi (H6956) — Kohathite; the clan name of Numbers 3-4 and 1 Chronicles 6.
Hebrew massa (H4853) — a burden, that which is borne; the burden of the sons of Kohath (Numbers 4:15).
Hebrew katheph (H3802) — shoulder; they should bear upon their shoulders (Numbers 7:9).
Hebrew mishpat — due order; we sought him not after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:13).
usage: They shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die (Numbers 4:15) — the terms of the highest Levitical office.
Because the service of the sanctuary… was that they should bear upon their shoulders (Numbers 7:9) — no wagons for the Kohathites.
None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites (1 Chronicles 15:2) — David, corrected, quoting the law back.

etymology: The descendants of Gershon, Levi’s firstborn, comprising the families of the Libnites and the Shimites (Numbers 3:21). They pitched behind the tabernacle westward and carried its curtains, coverings, and hangings — the fabric of the house of God.
biblical_def: The Gershonites are the eldest Levitical clan and the one given the least glamorous charge. The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward (Numbers 3:23), behind the holy place, with Eliasaph the son of Lael over them. Their burden was the textile of the sanctuary: they shall bear the curtains of the tabernacle, and the tabernacle of the congregation, his covering, and the covering of the badgers’ skins that is above upon it, and the hanging for the door (Numbers 4:25). Not the ark, not the altar, not the candlestick — the tent cloth, the ropes, and the door curtain. Two wagons and four oxen were given them for it (Numbers 7:7), while the Kohathites got none. And the charge is put under the same authority as every other: At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens, and in all their service (Numbers 4:27). In Hezekiah’s cleansing of the temple the Gershonites are there with the rest — of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah (2 Chronicles 29:12) — among the Levites who arose and sanctified themselves when a king finally opened the doors of the house of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no GERSHONITE entry. The name Gershon, also spelled Gershom, is generally connected with the Hebrew for a stranger or sojourner there — the same word behind the naming of Moses’ son.
webster_full: GERSHONITE, n. — A descendant of Gershon, the eldest son of Levi; one of the Levitical clan charged with the curtains and coverings of the tabernacle.
Numbers 3:21 names their two families: the Libnites and the Shimites.
The Authorized Version spells the name Gershon in Numbers and Gershom in 1 Chronicles 6:1 and 6:16; it is one man.
Two wagons and four oxen were assigned to their service (Numbers 7:7), the burden being bulky rather than holy.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; the biblical usage is confined to Numbers, Joshua 21, and Chronicles.
scriptures: Numbers 3:21
Of Gershon was the family of the Libnites, and the family of the Shimites: these are the families of the Gershonites.
Numbers 3:23
The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward.
Numbers 4:25

And they shall bear the curtains of the tabernacle, and the tabernacle of the congregation, his covering, and the covering of the badgers’ skins that is above upon it, and the hanging for the door of the tabernacle of the congregation,
Numbers 4:27

At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens, and in all their service: and ye shall appoint unto them in charge all their burdens.
2 Chronicles 29:12

Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God assigns the curtains as deliberately as He assigns the ark, and that the eldest son of Levi carried tent cloth by divine appointment and not by demotion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Gershon was Levi’s firstborn, and his sons carried the coverings while Kohath’s carried the ark. Scripture does not explain the arrangement; it simply records it as an appointment, and it names the Gershonites, their families, their prince, their camping place, and their exact inventory with the same care it uses for the holy vessels. Paul argues the same point at length about the body: the members which seem more feeble are necessary, and God has tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked. Congregations that publicly honour only their visible offices are contradicting a passage of Numbers as well as a chapter of 1 Corinthians.

The second thing to recover is that ordinary work in the house of God is still holy work under authority. Their burdens and their service were at the appointment of Aaron and his sons, assigned by name and by charge. There is no such thing in Scripture as a portion of church labour too mundane to be regulated, and no such thing as a servant of the sanctuary who reports to nobody. The curtains had to be numbered, carried, and set up in the right order, or the tabernacle could not stand. When Hezekiah cleansed the temple centuries later, the Gershonites were still there and still named, which is its own quiet commendation of a family that had done unspectacular work faithfully for a very long time.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gershon or Gershom (H1648), from ger a sojourner and sham there; the gentilic is Gershunni (H1649).
roots_lines: Hebrew Gershon (H1648) — Gershon, Gershom; the firstborn of Levi (Genesis 46:11).
Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a stranger; the element behind the name, as at Exodus 2:22.
Hebrew Gershunni (H1649) — Gershonite; Numbers 3-4, Joshua 21:33, 1 Chronicles 23:7.
Hebrew yeriah (H3407) — a curtain of the tabernacle; the chief item of their burden (Numbers 4:25).
Hebrew tachash (H8476) — badger, or the animal whose skins formed the outer covering (Numbers 4:25).
usage: Shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward (Numbers 3:23) — the appointed station of the eldest Levitical house.
They shall bear the curtains of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:25) — the fabric of the sanctuary as a sacred charge.
At the appointment of Aaron and his sons (Numbers 4:27) — ordinary service, still under authority.

etymology: The descendants of Merari, Levi’s third son, whose name is connected with the Hebrew for bitterness. Their charge was the frame of the tabernacle — boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pins, and cords — the heaviest burden and the least visible when the house was standing.
biblical_def: The Merarites carried the skeleton of the house of God. Under the custody and charge of the sons of Merari shall be the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and the sockets thereof, and all the vessels thereof, and all that serveth thereto (Numbers 3:36), and the charge is repeated at Numbers 4:31 with the pins and cords added. Four wagons and eight oxen were assigned them, twice what Gershon received, because the load was silver sockets and acacia boards overlaid with gold. Nothing they carried was ever seen once the tabernacle was pitched; the curtains covered the boards, and the boards held everything else up. The clan is one of the three named in the census of Levi: of Gershon, the family of the Gershonites: of Kohath, the family of the Kohathites: of Merari, the family of the Merarites (Numbers 26:57). They kept their office for a thousand years. When David set the singers over the service of song in the house of the LORD, Ethan the son of Kishi of the sons of Merari stood on the left hand with Asaph on the right and Heman in the midst. And when Hezekiah opened the temple doors, Kish the son of Abdi and Azariah the son of Jehalelel came up of the sons of Merari with the rest.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no MERARITE entry. The Hebrew Merari is generally traced to marar, to be bitter — the same root as Marah, Mara, and the bitter herbs of the passover.
webster_full: MERARITE, n. — A descendant of Merari, the third son of Levi; one of the Levitical clan charged with the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets of the tabernacle.
Numbers 3:33 names their two families: the Mahlites and the Mushites.
They pitched on the north side of the tabernacle, under Zuriel the son of Abihail (Numbers 3:35).
Four wagons and eight oxen were given to their service (Numbers 7:8), the load being the heaviest of the three clans.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; Numbers, Joshua 21, and 1 Chronicles 6 and 26 supply the biblical usage.
scriptures: Numbers 3:36

And under the custody and charge of the sons of Merari shall be the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and the sockets thereof, and all the vessels thereof, and all that serveth thereto,
Numbers 4:31

And this is the charge of their burden, according to all their service in the tabernacle of the congregation; the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and sockets thereof,
Numbers 26:57
And these are they that were numbered of the Levites after their families: of Gershon, the family of the Gershonites: of Kohath, the family of the Kohathites: of Merari, the family of the Merarites.
Numbers 10:21
And the Kohathites set forward, bearing the sanctuary: and the other did set up the tabernacle against they came.
2 Chronicles 29:12

Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the heaviest and least visible labour in the house of God is a named, numbered, divinely assigned office — not the residue left over when the honoured work is distributed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Numbers 10:21 contains a small, easily missed sentence: the Kohathites came forward bearing the sanctuary, and the other did set up the tabernacle against they came. The margin identifies the other as the Gershonites and Merarites. That is, the men carrying the boards went ahead, raised the frame, and had the house standing before the ark arrived. Nobody watching the procession was looking at them. Their work was finished before the holy things appeared and invisible the moment the curtains went on. Scripture nevertheless records their families, their prince, their wagons, their oxen, and their exact inventory down to the pins and the cords.

This is the pattern for how a church should think about its unseen labour, and Reformed churches with a high view of preaching are as capable as any of getting it wrong. The Merarites did not carry lesser things; they carried the things everything else rested on. Their descendants were still at their post when Hezekiah cleansed the temple and when David appointed the singers, and Ethan the Merarite stood beside Asaph in the service of song. A family that keeps an unglamorous charge for a thousand years has done something the church should know how to name. Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
roots_summary: Hebrew Merari (H4847), bitter, from marar (H4843) to be bitter; the gentilic is Merari used adjectivally, Merarite (H4848).
roots_lines: Hebrew Merari (H4847) — Merari; third son of Levi (Genesis 46:11; Exodus 6:16).
Hebrew marar (H4843) — to be bitter; the root also behind Marah (Exodus 15:23) and Naomi’s call me Mara.
Hebrew Merari (H4848) — Merarite; the clan name of Numbers 26:57 and 1 Chronicles 26:19.
Hebrew qeresh (H7175) — a board of the tabernacle; the chief item of their burden (Numbers 3:36).
Hebrew eden (H134) — a socket or base, of silver, into which the boards were set; the foundation of the whole structure.
usage: The boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof (Numbers 3:36) — the frame everything else rested on.
The other did set up the tabernacle against they came (Numbers 10:21) — the house standing before the ark arrived.
Of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi (2 Chronicles 29:12) — the clan still at its post under Hezekiah.
